title: Knowledge-rich or information-rich?
author: Paul Kirschner
summary: Paul Kirschner follows up on a Natalie Wexler post to clarify a distinction he says many educators, administrators and publishers miss: a knowledge-rich curriculum is not the same as an information-rich one. An information-rich curriculum offers abundant articles, topics and encounters but risks exposure without learning, while a knowledge-rich curriculum deliberately selects and sequences what pupils should know, remember and build on. He explains vertical coherence (cumulative build over years) and horizontal coherence (links across subjects), arguing that the former is the backbone and the latter only the connective tissue. He frames the case for knowledge richness as an equity argument, since pupils without background knowledge depend most on the curriculum to make connections explicit. He concludes that schools should aim for a curriculum knowledge-rich in structure and information-rich in texture.
points: Exposure is not learning: an information-rich curriculum can be full of stimuli yet thin in what pupils retain and understand.
Knowledge-rich does not mean fact-heavy but carefully structured, cumulatively designed intellectual architecture.
Vertical coherence is the curriculum's backbone, while horizontal or thematic coherence is only connective tissue and cannot substitute for sequencing.
Loose, weakly sequenced content disadvantages pupils with little background knowledge, making knowledge richness an equity issue.
The best design uses knowledge for the spine and information for the texture, so that information serves the growth of knowledge.
quotes: But exposure isn’t the same as learning. Pupils can come into contact with a large amount of information without storing very much of it in their long-term memory, and they can move from one interesting topic to the next without building secure understanding of the link between them. An information-rich curriculum can therefore be full in one sense and thin in another: full of stimuli, but thin in terms of what pupils actually come to know, understand, and retain.
It asks not merely what pupils might profitably encounter, but what they should know, remember, and be able to build upon later. That shift sounds small, but it changes everything.
Pupils don’t become better thinkers by hovering above knowledge, nor by being surrounded by information. They become better thinkers by knowing more, and by knowing more in organised ways.

But a good knowledge-rich curriculum isn’t about indiscriminate accumulation. It’s about intellectual architecture. It’s about making sure that the knowledge pupils meet is worth knowing. It’s about introducing facts and knowledge in an order that makes sense. And it’s about preparing the ground for later learning. Knowledge-rich, in other words, doesn’t mean fact-heavy so much as carefully structured and cumulatively designed.
As Christine Counsell and Steve Mastin from Opening Worlds say: ‘A knowledge-rich curriculum is a promise you make to future teachers about what their students have learned.
A beautifully linked project isn’t necessarily a well-sequenced education. Pupils may enjoy the connections within a project while still failing to build secure knowledge over time.

That is why horizontal coherence is best thought of as the connective tissue of the curriculum, not its backbone. It adds meaning and reinforcement, but cannot substitute for the careful sequencing that enables long-term intellectual growth.
